c.tagline: France's last outpost in North America - colorful, foggy, and Basque-Breton.

taxi.fareNote: There are no ride-hailing apps (no Uber or Bolt); a handful of local taxis are booked by phone. The town is small enough to cross on foot, so most visitors simply walk.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-standard emergency number; the French services also apply directly - 17 police, 18 fire, 15 medical (SAMU).

hood_landmark.Centre-ville (Downtown): Saint-Pierre Cathedral and the colorful harborfront around Place du Général de Gaulle
hood_landmark.Pointe aux Canons: the historic harbor-defense cannon battery and its little red-and-white lighthouse
hood_landmark.Île aux Marins: the abandoned fishing 'ghost village' and its 1874 Notre-Dame-des-Marins church
hood_landmark.Savoyard: windswept Anse de Savoyard cove and coastal walking paths
hood_landmark.Anse à Henry / Cap à l'Aigle: the Anse à Henry archaeological site, with traces of indigenous settlement going back millennia, below seabird cliffs

hoods: Anse à Henry / Cap à l'Aigle
hood_desc: The compact harbor-front core around the Place du Général de Gaulle, lined with brightly painted wooden houses, French bakeries, cafes, wine shops, and the cathedral; where nearly everything - hotels, restaurants, and the ferry pier - sits within a short walk.

The scenic point guarding the harbor entrance, marked by the red-and-white Pointe aux Canons lighthouse and its old cannon battery; a favorite waterfront stroll with views back over the colorful town.

A tiny former fishing island just across the harbor, now a preserved open-air museum village of restored houses, a church, and the Archipélitude museum; inhabited only in summer and reached by a short passenger-boat hop.
A quiet traditional fishing hamlet on the western side of Saint-Pierre island, with simple homes and a slower, local pace away from the town center.

The rugged northern edge of Saint-Pierre island around the Anse à Henry cove and Cap à l'Aigle, with hiking trails, freshwater ponds, seabirds, and windswept Atlantic scenery; a nature escape rather than a place to stay.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the archipelago.

transit.hours: No scheduled public bus network; the town is compact and walkable, and taxis run on call.
transit.note: Saint-Pierre has no bus, metro, or tram system - the town is small enough to cross on foot in 20-30 minutes. A few taxis and rental cars cover longer trips and the airport.
transit.pay: Taxis are paid in cash (euros); there is no transit card or fare system.

air: Saint-Pierre Pointe Blanche Airport (FSP) - Air Saint-Pierre

transit.m: Taxi into town (5-10 min); many guesthouses offer free pickup

tip.r: French custom applies - service is included in the bill, so tipping is not expected; rounding up or leaving small change for good service is appreciated.

landmarks: Île aux Marins (Sailors' Island)
A hauntingly preserved abandoned fishing village across the harbour, its wooden church, schoolhouse and scattered houses frozen in Atlantic time.
Pointe aux Canons Lighthouse
The little red-and-white harbour lighthouse beside old shore batteries, Saint-Pierre's most photographed emblem guarding the entrance to France's North American port.
Cathédrale de Saint-Pierre
The archipelago's basalt-fronted cathedral, rebuilt after fire with Alsatian stained glass gifted by de Gaulle, blending Basque and Breton heritage.
L'Arche Musée et Archives
A striking modern museum tracing the archipelago's cod-fishing saga, Prohibition rum-running boom and the only guillotine ever used in North America.
Musée Héritage
A charmingly packed private museum of period pharmacy, schoolroom and Prohibition-era artefacts recounting daily life in France's last North American territory.
Les Salines
A photogenic row of brightly painted fishing shacks and drying stages along the shore, keeping the memory of the great cod fishery alive.
Fronton Zazpiak-Bat
The town's Basque pelota court, heart of summer festivals that celebrate the islanders' Basque roots with games, music and dancing.
Place du Général de Gaulle
Saint-Pierre's central square ringed by colourful clapboard facades, host to markets and commemorations of de Gaulle's famous 1967 visit.
Phare de Galantry (Galantry Lighthouse)
The clifftop lighthouse on Saint-Pierre's southern heights, where foghorns sound over seabird colonies and sweeping North Atlantic panoramas.
Quai de la République Waterfront
The harbourfront promenade of jaunty multicoloured houses and fishing boats that gives Saint-Pierre its distinctly French seaside-village charm.

train.note: There is no railway in this small French archipelago off Newfoundland. Arrive by air into Saint-Pierre Airport, with flights from Montreal, Halifax and St John's, or by the seasonal ferry from Canada.

bus.note: No coach routes - the islands are tiny and have only a few kilometres of road. There is no public bus network; taxis and rental cars cover Saint-Pierre town, and most people walk. Note that the islands use the euro and French rules, despite being 25 km from Canada.

ferry.note: The Fortune crossing to Newfoundland is a genuine international sailing between France and Canada, taking about 90 minutes and running roughly May to September only - outside that season you fly. Carry your passport; French and Canadian immigration both apply. The Miquelon boat is the domestic link between the two main islands. Sailings are frequently disrupted by North Atlantic fog and swell.

half.name: Miquelon-Langlade
half.blurb: A ferry about an hour away reaches this quieter island of sand dunes, lagoons, and free-roaming horses connected by a narrow isthmus.

half.name: Fortune, Newfoundland
half.blurb: A ferry across international waters reaches this small Canadian fishing town, the closest mainland North American port to Saint-Pierre.
